utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Mladen Naletilic and Vinko Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have the next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Examined by Mr. Par:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I start my examination today, I would like to inform you that you have been granted protective measures and that is face distortion and a pseudonym. I am now going to give you a paper with your name on it. If this is indeed your name, just say yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can we please go to private session for the first few questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, let us start with the time of the Serbian aggression against Mostar. Let us remind ourselves of that period. You said that you lived in the eastern part of Mostar. Can you please briefly tell us something about that time? How did you live in the eastern part of Mostar? What happened to you? Did you have any military engagement and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: With my wife, I lived in that part of the city, and my apartment was in the vicinity of the barracks called Northern Camp, where the Serbian Army forces were, they had arrived already in 1991, in the territory of Mostar. On their arrival, the safety and security situation changed in Mostar from what it used to be before that. There was shooting every night from the surrounding hills, where the Serbian soldiers were, and very often we would hear shots from the barracks, which served to intimidate the population. So it was not easy to live in that part of the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was an atmosphere of insecurity. However, there were Serbs, Muslims and Croats living there. Did they show the same attitude towards the Serbian aggression or were there any differences between them? Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: All the Serbs, more or less, were in favour of the arrival of the Serbian reservists and Croats and Muslims had a different attitude towards that and they did not accept that because it was no longer the Yugoslav Army but the Serbian Army. 99 per cent of the members of this army were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did Muslims and Croats do in the eastern part of Mostar? Did they start leaving the city or did they organise military units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: In this part of the city, Croats and Muslims started leaving, either for other parts of the town. They crossed the river and went to stay with relatives or family. The situation in this part of the city was no longer safe. Everybody's life was at risk so everybody tried to find a safer place to live.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are saying that the situation was the way it was and that's why they moved to the western part of the town. What was -- what was it that made the western part of the city safer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: In that part of the city, there were no members of the Serbian Army. They were in the eastern part, in the barracks, and in the western part, there was no Serbian Army. Some legal police forces started being organised. They were armed, there were patrols, so it was much safer for Croats and Muslims to be in that part of the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is the period of insecurity. Did you personally, with your family, move to the western part of the city? And where did you cross? Where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: I moved to this other apartment that I had just shown you. This is where my mother-in-law lived, and together with my wife, I went there and lived with my mother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you arrived in the western part, did you have any military engagement? Were you mobilised? Were you a member of any military unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: When the conflict with the Serbian Army started, that is the conflict between the Serbian Army and the armed people or the police, then I did not have any military engagement. But after a certain period of time, I was mobilised. I received my call-up papers. So I enlisted with the HVO, which was at the time the only military formation in that part of the town. However, it was not a military engagement. That happened actually after the conflict, when the Serbian forces were forced to leave the eastern part. I was then engaged because some parts of the town were in rubble and I, as an architect, could assess the damage, so I was given a work obligation and that was to assess different facilities, public facilities, monuments, and to assess the extent of damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I have understood you well, you are now in the western part of Mostar, the war went on for a while, and then stopped, and you were engaged by enlisting and by being given a work obligation to assess the damage in Mostar. Can you tell me how you assessed the damage inflicted by the Serbian aggression and did you compile some documents to document that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: Personally, I went to every facility, to every building, together with photographers. We made photographic documentation. And I, as a result of that, am the author of a book called, "Mostar, Urbicide 1992. These groups involved Muslims and Serbs, the ones who had remained in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that book contains data on the damage inflicted during the aggression by the Serbs. Can you tell us in brief what kind of damage did you encounter in Mostar after the Serbian aggression? Did the majority of objects suffer damage and what kind of damage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise to the witness for the interruption and to counsel but this is testimony that requires or is based upon a specialised knowledge of the witness, based upon a rather unique experience, not referred to in the least in the witness summary that we've been provided. I think it's potentially an important, certainly an interesting subject, but it's not one which I'm in the least prepared to cross-examine about. There has been testimony in this trial on that subject, and we are just -- we simply have had no notice that this was going to be an area for the direct examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Par, we would like to know the relevance of this issue, that is the damage inflicted during the aggression by the Serbs with this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that was part of the indictment, and a lot of other things my client is being charged with, one of them the destruction of monuments and this was also the subject of the witnesses for the Prosecution. I don't intend to dwell upon that but I cannot not ask the witness, who was there at the time, about the results of his work. My intention was to ask the witness about the things that he did as part of his military engagement. I just wanted him to tell us Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. whether the majority of objects were destroyed or not. I don't wish to waste a lot of time but to have a witness like this and not to ask him a question like that, I don't consider possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I don't wish to suggest that anyone other than Mr. Par should determine the scope of his direct, but if we could go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Serbian aggression is now over. After the Serbian aggression, did you go back to your apartment or did you stay with your mother-in-law in the western part of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: I and my wife stayed with my mother-in-law because the conditions of life in the other part of the city were rather bad. There was no electricity. There was no water. There was a lot of destruction. So the conditions for return were not in place. Our apartment was also damaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go there from time to time? When did you go there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: Usually on weekends my wife and myself would go there, stay there, clean a little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time when you went to that apartment, did you notice any changes in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: In that part of Mostar, some new people appeared, some that I had never seen before. Those were Muslims from the areas under the control of the Serbian Army who had been expelled from Trebinje, Bileca and other cities from Eastern Herzegovina. These people had been expelled, they arrived in East Mostar and then they entered the empty apartments. That's why me and my wife would go there so often, to make sure that nobody forcefully breaks into it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now let me take you to the 9th of May, 1993, the conflict between Muslims and Croats started in Mostar. Where were you exactly on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: It was a Sunday, and I've already said that my wife and me were in our apartment quite often on weekends. We were there around 5.00 or 6.00 in the morning, the shooting started. I didn't know what it was all about, and then we heard via the media what was going on, at least some things I learned. I didn't leave my apartment. I was in my apartment all the time. I basically didn't know what the whole thing was all about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the war started on the 9th of May. You were in your apartment in East Mostar. Did anybody knock on your door, the army? Were you disturbed? Did you leave the apartment? What happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: Soldiers came to my apartment. They didn't ring the bell. They tried to break in by pushing the door by foot. There was -- my name was on the door. They went around the building. They threatened to kill anybody, me including, if they found any weapons or ammunition. Then my neighbours also came and they shouted, saying that I'm an Ustasha, that all Ustashas should be killed, slaughtered. They told me not to leave the apartment and that I was in house prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the 9th of May, how long did you stay in that apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: I think three weeks, some 20 days, I stayed in the apartment. I lost 20 kilos during that period of time. I didn't sleep. I developed psoriasis, which was stress related.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did your wife take it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: My wife suffered some psychological problems, which in my case reflected on my skin, and in her case, she was depressed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after the 20 days that you spent there under certain pressure, you finally decided to leave the apartment. Did you leave it and where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: Via the media that we could listen to and those were small portable radios, I learned that 20 days later the conflict had started, that there was UNPROFOR on some of the lines and that we were given an opportunity to be taken by buses to the other part of the town. So I decided to move to West Mostar together with my wife, who was by then in a very bad health condition. I knew more or less the location from which the buses departed. That was close to the Razvitak department store so that's how we decided to leave. We picked up some clothes and things and we went to the place of departure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this bus journey was organised in a certain way. My question is: Was it organised in the presence of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: UNPROFOR just escorted and provided security for these buses, but it was the BH Army soldiers who entered the buses and they were the ones who made decisions as to who could cross and who couldn't. At one point, they wanted to take me off the bus. However, I knew some people on the other side. At that time they helped me to remain on the bus and to cross the river together with my wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when we are talking about time, when would that have been?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: End of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you and your wife crossed over to the other side. Could you please tell us what was the ethnic background of your wife?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: She was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your mother-in-law, living in the western part of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to live with your mother-in-law in that other apartment in western part of Mostar, in May, 1993, did you engage yourself militarily in the western parts of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: To start with, no. Again, I registered myself for the work obligation for about a month, and then I got a call-up papers, mobilisation papers and I responded and I was engaged militarily in a military unit from those parts of town that I knew. And it was known as the 4th Battalion. That's how it was organised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 4th Battalion, in the 4th Battalion, what were your tasks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: I was a soldier who was standing guard in one part of the town, towards the Hum hill. We were securing that part of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, at that time, in that building where you lived, where your mother-in-law lived, were there any cases that in that neighbourhood, that some Muslims were forced out? Did you hear about it or did your mother-in-law tell you about it? Could you please elaborate on the atmosphere, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: She told me of course, when we arrived, that many neighbours who were there in that part of town, that they had been expelled, but that she had also been approached by some men who came to her apartment, looked into her apartment, saw that there was nobody in the apartment, and realised there was nobody there and then they left. They didn't harm her or her neighbour, who was also Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But when you were in that apartment, with your mother-in-law, were there also soldiers who came to the door, checking who was in the apartment and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: On several occasions, soldiers came whom I didn't know personally, and they came to check something but when they saw that I was in uniform, that I had a rifle, then they would normally return.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did they introduce themselves if they did at all, when they came?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: I didn't ask many questions. They would normally go back as soon as they saw me that I was a Croat, that I was engaged, then they would go back, but I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, did you know Vinko Martinovic, Stela?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: I knew Vinko from before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the nature of your relationship? How did you meet? Where did you know him from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: Vinko's brother Jadranko and myself worked together in a company. So we had business relations, and then through Vinko's brother Jadranko I met Vinko and his parents, mother and father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, when you were in the western part of town, did you hear stories about Stela and his soldiers are expelling people from apartments? Did you hear such stories?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were cases that you've heard about cases that people were falsely representing themselves as members of Vinko's unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about it and I personally had an experience in 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us about your personal experience in relation to these stories?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: Among other things, these people who came to the door, these unknown men who came to the door, in 1996, I decided to return from Germany because in 1994, after Mr. Koschnik came, when Mostar was normalised again, and when I felt that I could leave my mother-in-law, because my wife was already in Germany, I then went to Germany, and I was there for two years. When my wife and I decided to go back, which was sometime in 1996, it was in October, 1996, so we made all the preparations to go back, but I received a call from my neighbour that some men had entered this apartment where we had been, which I had located on the map, where we were supposed to go back to, and because my mother-in-law wasn't Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there in that apartment, she had gone to see her sister -- to her sister's in Croatia, they found out that this was an empty apartment and three armed soldiers, this -- I heard from my next door neighbour who is also a Muslim, because she reacted when they started to break the door down. So they forced her and they said, "We are Stela's men. You shouldn't interfere." And so on. So they forced her to back down. And then she called me in Germany and told me that they introduced themselves as being Stela's men and that's when I called Jadranko because I had good relationship with him, I knew Jadranko was Vinko's brother so I asked him to check whether these soldiers were truly Stela's men and whether something could be done in this respect. And then Jadranko told me he would find out he promised he would inform himself at Vinko's who these people were and if I could call him in a few days. A few days later I called Jadranko and Jadranko told me that he had spoken to Vinko and that he didn't know these soldiers at all. I found out that one of the soldiers was called Delinac and that he came from the vicinities of Konjic. And so on. So Jadranko said that in that unit, Vinko's unit, there were no soldiers from Konjic, particularly not with this name or surname. That's why I personally had to come from Germany. And then on the basis of my contacts and people I knew in the police, and in politics, they helped me evict these people from the apartment. Or, well, specifically that man who was in the apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And today, you live in that apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where does your mother-in-law live?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: My mother-in-law lives in this eastern part of town where I used to live with my now ex-wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the war made you exchange places? You as a Croat went to live in the western part and stayed in that apartment and she, as a Muslim, went to the eastern part in your former apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have finished my examination-in-chief. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Stringer:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, just a few questions. You said that when you returned to East Mostar, this is the period before the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats in Mostar, there was a point when you returned to East Mostar and you found that there were now a lot of Muslims who had arrived, who had come from other parts of Eastern Herzegovina because those parts had been taken by the Serbs. Do you recall that? You have to answer verbally.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that they were living in empty apartments, those Muslims who had come from other areas were living in empty apartments in Mostar. My question, sir, is whether those were empty apartments because they were apartments that had formerly belonged to Serbs who were now no longer living in Mostar after the liberation of Mostar in June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did a lot of Serbs leave Mostar during the course of the Serb aggression and then, in the period after the liberation of Mostar, in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: And before the war, before the war started. By the very arrival of Serb units, many Serb families started to leave Mostar. And in relation to your other part of the question, in that eastern part of town, most of the apartments were Serbian. So these were apartments of the Serbs who had left, that withdrew with the Serb Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified -- moving forward now to the period of time in which you were talking about the experience of living in West Mostar, you said that you heard from your mother in law that, I think many of her neighbours, her Muslim neighbours, had been expelled from their flats in West Mostar. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, sir, that she was able to keep that flat in West Mostar throughout the conflict because her son-in-law was a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: Obviously these people who came to the door did not know me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were uniformed, you were wearing an HVO patch on your shoulder, I take it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: Yes, but that happened later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That's what I want to ask. Maybe I should do a better job of setting the time frame. The time frame that I'm interested in is the period of 1993, after the 9th of May. In fact, after the end of May, which is when I believe you moved across into West Mostar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, from the end of May of 1993, until the end of the conflict, is that the period of time in which your mother-in-law spoke of many Muslims being evicted from their flats in West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: No. Can I speak?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: Not that part but this other part. So when I came to this apartment, she told me about what had happened when I wasn't there, because when I was already there on that other side, then I of course knew what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to just try to clarify this a little bit. You returned to West Mostar or you went over to West Mostar at the end of May, 1993, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sometime shortly thereafter, you were again mobilised into the HVO and became a member of the 4th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. My question is this: Your mother would have been expelled in 1993, your mother-in-law would have bee expelled in 1993 if she hadn't -- if you had not been living with her and if you had not been a member of the HVO. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I would object to that question. It calls for speculation. Pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: There question has been asked before. I think at this moment, the Prosecutor is just making clear the instance of this question. Witness, you may answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not quite clear about what the question was. Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1993, your mother-in-law would have been expelled from West Mostar, just like all the other Muslims --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: No, no. She wasn't expelled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: She would have been --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: She remained in her apartment. She remained in her apartment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stringer, ask the reason why his mother-in-law was not evicted from her apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was your mother-in-law not evicted at a time when all the other Muslims were being evicted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: I can only assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to that question, the form of that question assumes facts not in evidence. This witness has already testified his mother-in-law told him that some of her neighbours got evicted. The question if you look at it assumes that all Muslims were evicted. I object to the form of the question. It assumes facts not in evidence, calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek, this witness is your witness. It's not your witness. So you have no right to interrupt in the proceedings. Witness, you may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was she allowed to remain when the other Muslims were not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: I don't know. I suppose because she was an elderly woman that they left her there. She was on her own and they realised that there was nobody else in the apartment so they then went back. They probably didn't feel that she was posing a threat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I suggest to you, sir, that she was allowed to remain because she had you there as a member of the HVO to protect her?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: I was not there. I was -- when the conflict started, she -- I was in the eastern part of town, in my apartment. She was in the western part in her apartment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, I don't know if you want to pursue this any further but perhaps to clarify the matter you should say to the witness, after he and his wife arrived at his mother-in-law's apartment, did his presence there play any role in his mother-in-law's as a Muslim being permitted to remain there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you hear the question or the suggestion of Judge Clark? I think rather than muddy the water by attempting to repeat it -- go ahead and answer the question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: So in this period, when I was not in that apartment, I could not have had any influence on whether she would remain or be expelled but when I was in the apartment, I was able to. And normally I tried. Of course I did my best for her to remain there with me and not to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now my last question again, just to be sure, the story that you tell of when these persons came and identified themselves as Stelici, that was three years later or so, in 1996, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Mr. President, just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please. Re-examined by Mr. Par:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just a couple of questions in relation to the situation regarding the Muslims in western part of Mostar. In this house, in this building where your mother-in-law lived, when you arrived at the end of May, 1993, were there other Muslims there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was, for instance, a Muslim? [redacted] who had informed me in Germany. She was there throughout the war. [redacted]. She was there with her husband and her two children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, in Mostar, were there other Muslims? Did you see them? Did you know that there were other Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: There were, because all of us had either a friend or a husband, wife, a spouse, everybody had a family relations, and people were protecting each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you compare this, what you have lived through, in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. relation to these pressures, evictions and so on in the eastern part of Mostar, and what you heard that happened in the western part of Mostar, there in eastern against Croats, in western against Muslims, do you see any kind of difference? What was going on? Was it similar, was it very different?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: What I saw, what I lived through, and the way I saw the war, on the eastern part, I presume that my mother-in-law and these people felt in a similar way on this other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions from Judges? Judge Clark. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Could I ask you a few questions, Witness MR? You described how after you came to the west side to live with your mother-in-law, that on a number of occasions soldiers came to the door. When they came to the door, did they identify themselves? Did they say why they were there? Can you describe that in a little detail, what you remember of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: I did not know these soldiers. These were men whom I didn't know. But you can assume that nobody will want to identify themselves as they are ringing the bell at the door of someone's apartment wanting to force their way in but once they entered the apartment I would let them come in, and when I appear in uniform and a rifle, normally then they would just leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: What I wanted to know is when they knocked it at the door, did they identify the unit that they belonged to or the orders that they had or did they seem to you to be on a personal, illegal mission?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: I presumed that this -- this is the second part of the -- second version. They came for their own personal reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: During the war between the HVO and the Muslim army, did you hear many stories about illegal activity and the expulsion of your Muslim neighbours, Muslim people generally, in the west part?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Were the stories always about Stelici or about other people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: It was always about Stelici. They were people who -- they were the usual suspects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: The period that you give us specific evidence on in 1996 referred to soldiers from a certain part of Herzegovina who came to the apartment that your mother-in-law lived in. That intrigues me somewhat, that people would be called Stelici so long after the war. Was Mr. Martinovic still commander or involved with the military or in paramilitary unit at that stage, in 1996?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: Well, I can't know that, because from 1994 to 1996, I was in Germany. I didn't have an insight into the situation in the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: But you said that you spoke to his brother Jadranko, and that he was able to say that Vinko Martinovic said that he didn't have people of that name in his unit. So does that presuppose the existence or the continued existence of a paramilitary unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: I cannot know that, because I spoke to Vinko's brother on the phone and I don't know whether that unit existed then. But I called because these people introduced themselves as Stelici but whether the units existed at all at that time, I don't know, because it was already in 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You said that you then sought the assistance of political friends you had and some people in the police to evict them. Does that mean that you weren't able to go to court and get an eviction order, that it had to be done by some degree of influence rather than by rule of law?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MR
utterances.text: Since there were no established courts at that time, and there was the European Union administration, as the institution that was there for any complaints, I tried to do this in a legal way of sorts. So it was through the police, through some institutions of authority, so that I wouldn't clash with this man. I wanted the police, the authorities, to take care of this. The administration that was managing the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judge's questions? Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, thank you very much for coming to give your evidence. When the usher pulls down the blinds, she will show you out of the room. We all wish you a good future. At this stage are there any documents to tender? Yes, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. The map that the witness marked, marked two locations, and this is D2/50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'll give the floor to Madam Registrar. She has to correct the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The pseudonym sheets is D2/50 and the map is D2/51, both under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much, these two documents are admitted into evidence. My suggestion is that we break now and we will continue with another witness in the next sitting. I was reminded to ask the Defence counsel what is the protective measures for the next witness? If there is any protective measures, we have to make the arrangement during the break. Yes, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For this witness, Mr. President, the Defence has asked for protective measures of a closed session. I hope that the Trial Chamber received this request yesterday. We spoke about this a few days ago. So this is the witness for whom we are asking a closed session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the next witness will be handled by Mr. Poriouvaev.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Par, your request is granted. So we will conduct the testimony of the next witness in the closed session. But I have to remind you that you should try your best to talk with your witness so that we could hear some witnesses in open session in the future proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will immediately express myself on this issue. I believe that this is the last witness who asked for a closed session. From out of all the witnesses, we only had two with closed sessions. The next few witnesses that we have left, and I believe that we have fewer than ten minutes, two will ask for the usual protective measures, maybe two or three, the pseudonym and the face distortion, while the others will testify in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. We will resume at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Since the closed session is granted, we will go to the closed session for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: 12.54 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 9th day of September, 2002, at 2.15 p.m. 25
